<p>After receiving the news of pregnancy, one of the first questions that comes to couples' minds, but which they are most ashamed to ask the doctor, is this: <em>"Can our sex life continue, or will it harm the baby?"</em></p><p>There are so many myths and fears surrounding this topic that many couples distance themselves from each other for 9 months. Some fear the baby will "feel" them, while others worry about injury. Let's break these taboos and clarify when sexual intercourse during pregnancy is safe and when it is risky, based on medical facts.</p><h2>The main question: Does it harm the baby?</h2><p>Short answer: <strong>No.</strong></p><p>If your pregnancy is proceeding normally and no specific restrictions have been set by your doctor, sexual intercourse is completely safe for your baby.</p><p>Your baby is inside a very secure "fortress" in the mother's womb:</p><ul><li><p><strong>Amniotic fluid:</strong> Acts as a "cushion" protecting the baby from impacts.</p></li><li><p><strong>Uterine muscles:</strong> Strong walls surround the baby.</p></li><li><p><strong>Mucus plug:</strong> Seals the cervix, preventing infections from entering.</p></li></ul><blockquote><p>Myth: "The baby knows or feels what is happening during intercourse."</p></blockquote><p>Truth: The baby does not understand what is happening. They may only feel an increase in the mother's heart rate and a slight rocking motion, as if in a cradle.</p><p>&gt;</p><h2>Pregnancy trimesters and sexual desire (Libido)</h2><p>It is normal for your sexual desire to rise and fall like a "roller coaster" throughout pregnancy.</p><ul><li><p><strong>1st Trimester (Fatigue period):</strong> Sexual desire may decrease due to nausea (morning sickness), weakness, and breast tenderness. During this period, many women simply want to sleep.</p></li><li><p><strong>2nd Trimester (Honeymoon):</strong> Your energy returns, and nausea passes. Due to increased blood flow to the pelvic organs, many women experience higher libido and more intense sensations during this period.</p></li><li><p><strong>3rd Trimester (Search for comfort):</strong> As the belly grows, movement becomes difficult and back pain occurs. Sexual desire may decrease again, but this does not apply to everyone.</p></li></ul><p></p><h2>When to say "NO"? (Medical Contraindications)</h2><p>In some cases, your doctor may prescribe <strong>"pelvic rest"</strong>. These are instances where sexual intercourse and even orgasm are prohibited:</p><h3>1. Risk of miscarriage or bleeding</h3><p>If you are in the early stages of pregnancy and have unexplained vaginal bleeding, spotting, or severe cramps, your doctor will prohibit sexual intercourse until the situation stabilizes.</p><h3>2. Placenta Previa (Low-lying placenta)</h3><p>This is when the placenta is located low and covers the cervix completely or partially. Sexual intercourse can cause serious bleeding. If this diagnosis is made, sexual intercourse is strictly prohibited until delivery.</p><h3>3. Cervical insufficiency (Incompetent cervix)</h3><p>If the cervix shortens or opens prematurely, sexual intercourse can trigger preterm labor.</p><h3>4. Risk of premature birth</h3><p>If you have had a premature birth in previous pregnancies or if your contractions have started early in this pregnancy, caution is necessary. The <strong>prostaglandins</strong> in semen can soften the cervix and accelerate labor.</p><h3>5. Rupture of membranes (Water breaking)</h3><p>If your water has broken or there is a leak, it means the barrier protecting the baby has been breached. In this case, sexual intercourse poses a serious <strong>risk of infection</strong>.</p><h2>Frequently asked concerns</h2><h3>"There was bleeding after intercourse, is this normal?"</h3><p>During pregnancy, the cervix is better supplied with blood and becomes more sensitive. Light, pink spotting after intercourse can be considered normal. However, if the bleeding is like a menstrual period or is accompanied by pain, <strong>consult a doctor immediately.</strong></p><h3>"Does orgasm start labor?"</h3><p>In a normal pregnancy, uterine contractions (Braxton Hicks) that occur during orgasm are harmless and pass quickly. However, in the final days of pregnancy (closer to the 40th week), some doctors recommend sexual intercourse to start labor naturally (due to the softening effect of semen).</p><h2>Tips for Safety and Comfort</h2><ul><li><p><strong>Positions:</strong> As your belly grows, face-to-face positions may become uncomfortable. The "spooning" (side-lying) position or positions where the woman is on top are more comfortable as they do not put pressure on the belly.</p></li><li><p><strong>Avoid lying on your back:</strong> After the 20th week, lying on your back can compress the "inferior vena cava," which can cause dizziness and reduce blood flow to the baby.</p></li><li><p><strong>Communication:</strong> Tell your partner and stop if you feel any discomfort or pain.</p></li></ul><p></p><p>Pregnancy is a special period where feelings of femininity and motherhood combine. Sexual life is a natural part of this period, and if there is no medical prohibition, there is no need to give it up. On the contrary, it can strengthen your emotional bond with your partner.</p><p>If you have doubts, do not hesitate to consult your doctor. And remember, intimacy is not just about sexual intercourse—hugging, massaging, and spending time together are also ways to show your love.</p><p><strong>Note:</strong> If you feel any unusual symptoms related to your pregnancy (pain, bleeding, water leaking), record them in the <strong>Anacan app</strong> and contact your doctor immediately.</p>
